one_liner: Plain Java tree-walking evaluator over a prebuilt AST on HotSpot 27, about 1.3x faster than the suite's C++ std::visit plus std::unordered_map version.
what_it_does: LangArena's Calculator::Interpreter test evaluates a generated 35,011-line arithmetic program whose AST is built once in prepare() (untimed). Each of the 100 timed passes creates a fresh interpreter, walks every statement recursively, and keeps variables in a string-keyed hash map: HashMap<String,Long> with boxed values in Java (instanceof chain over four node classes), std::unordered_map<std::string,int64_t> with std::visit over a std::variant in C++. It is a benchmark program, not a library; the 107-line Java file is the whole evaluator.
how_it_is_fast: Per pass both sides do 173,250 integer operations, 107,977 variable lookups and 35,011 inserts into a map that grows from empty (counts from replaying the suite's generator). The gap sits in the map: C++ hashes the std::string key on every find and operator[] call, reduces it with libstdc++'s prime-modulo bucket index, allocates one node per insert and frees all 35,011 nodes when the map dies inside the timed loop, while Java's String caches its hash code (the AST's name strings were hashed during warm-up), HashMap masks with a power of two and dead maps are reclaimed by the young collector (mechanism inferred from the sources, not measured by the suite). The win is not specific to a JIT: C# compiled ahead of time with NativeAOT (0.501 s) and Go (0.632 s) also beat every C/C++ row.
when_to_use: Choosing a runtime for an expression evaluator, rules engine or small scripting layer that walks a resident AST and keeps variables in a string-keyed map: idiomatic Java on HotSpot 27 ran 5.2 ms per 35,011-statement pass against 6.9 ms for the best C++ build.

JVM deployments that can pick the collector: with -XX:+UseSerialGC -Xmx512m the same code ran 0.364 s, about 1.9x faster than the best C/C++ row and 1.4x faster than default G1 (derived from page data).

As a reference point when a C++ interpreter keys its environment by std::string in std::unordered_map: the measured gap points at hashing and node allocation, which interning names to integer slots would remove on either side.
when_not_to_use: As a stable win: the lead over the best C/C++ row was 0.99x on 2026-07-14 (Java 0.692 s vs C++/G++/PGO 0.688 s, Java slower), 1.02x on 08-14, 1.03x on 09-03, 1.13x on 09-18 and 1.33x only on 2026-10-05 with Temurin 27 and a new host install (derived from the results files).
Memory-tight processes: Java/OpenJDK peaked at 239 MB RSS against 28 MB for C++/G++.
When an AOT binary is required: C#/AOT (NativeAOT, 0.501 s, 55 MB) already beats both Java/OpenJDK and every C++ row on this test, so the JIT is not what wins.
Short-lived processes: JVM startup and 20 warm-up passes are untimed for every language.
As a reason to rewrite an optimized interpreter: no C++ variant with an open-addressing map, interned variable slots or reserve() was measured.

integration.form: runtime plus source snippet (one Java file in a Maven project, java/src/main/java/benchmarks/CalculatorInterpreter.java, reusing the AST classes of CalculatorAst.java)
integration.dependencies: none for the evaluator (java.util only); the suite's harness reads its config through a JSON library (getJSONObject calls in Benchmark.java)
integration.min_toolchain: measured on Temurin OpenJDK 27+35; the code uses only java.util APIs available since Java 8 (Map.getOrDefault), the Maven target level was not checked
integration.platforms: any JVM platform; measured on x86-64 Linux (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each pass builds its own Interpreter with an unsynchronized HashMap, the shared AST is read-only

gotchas: The C++ baseline relies on undefined behaviour: replaying the generator shows 21,866 signed int64 overflows per pass in + - and * (values grow multiplicatively through 'v + (v + v) * v' lines); Java defines wraparound, and GCC and Clang happen to emit wrapping instructions, so the checksum 38749936 matches (reproduced exactly by the replay), but a C++ evaluator for this language should use unsigned or __builtin_*_overflow arithmetic.

Collector choice moves the result more than the language does: Java/OpenJDK default G1 0.52 s, SerialGC -Xmx512m 0.364 s, ParallelGC 'Opt' row 0.588 s; GraalVM JIT with default GC 0.663 s is barely ahead of C++ (0.691 s).

Same-file regressions show run-to-run sensitivity: C#/JIT moved from 0.54 s (2026-09-18, .NET 10) to 0.67 s (2026-10-05, .NET 11 rc.1) while the C++/G++ prod row stayed at 0.69-0.72 s across all five runs checked; one measurement per configuration, no variance.

The checksum adds only each pass's final value, but every statement feeds the next through v(n-1), so no work can be skipped; the Java and C++ simpleDiv/simple_mod are semantically identical (truncating division, zero divisor returns 0).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick the Calculator::Ast sibling instead when you want a clear managed-runtime win (1.66x, stable 1.35-1.66x across five runs); this entry is the weaker, newer case and mainly useful next to the Etc::Words and Etc::CacheSimulation siblings as another string-keyed std::unordered_map loss, while the kostya/benchmarks Brainfuck siblings (Scala and C# staged, 2.7-2.9x) show what closure compilation rather than plain tree walking buys.
verified_claims_summary: LangArena results of 2026-10-05 (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Linux) time 100 evaluations of a 35,011-statement AST after 20 warm-up passes: Java on Temurin OpenJDK 27 (java -Xmx2g, default G1) 0.52 s vs C++ with libstdc++ std::unordered_map at -O2 (g++ 16.0.1 trunk) 0.691 s, which is also the best of 16 Clang 22/GCC 16 C and C++ builds, about 1.33x (derived from page data); the -O3 'Fast' row is 0.705 s and the best C row (uthash) 1.067 s.
status_note: LangArena is active (MIT, 41 stars, 622 commits, monthly result files) and the Java evaluator has been unchanged since 2026-02-23; it is copyable, but the result is new and thin (under 1.13x before JDK 27, a loss on 2026-07-14) and measures hash-map and GC behaviour more than JIT code quality.
